Where Should Learning Live? Regret Analysis for Text, Parameter, and Joint Adaptation

Jungtaek Kim Affiliation: University of Arkansas    Jaden Park Affiliation: University of Wisconsin–Madison    Jongwon Jeong Affiliation: University of Wisconsin–Madison    Emmanouil-Vasileios Vlatakis-Gkaragkounis ††thanks: Co-corresponding authors. Affiliation: University of Wisconsin–Madison    Kangwook Lee11footnotemark: 1 Affiliation: KRAFTON Affiliation: Ludo Robotics
Abstract

Language-model systems can select prompts and parameter adapters repeatedly during deployment, using feedback to guide later choices. Earlier choices may change the context or environment inherited by later configurations. We study selection among preconstructed candidates and compare cumulative loss with the best fixed prompt–parameter pair used from the beginning. This excess loss separates into three terms: selection regret within the available family, the gap from restricting that family, and the benefit or harm of the actual deployment history. Selection is evaluated using the history each candidate would have produced if used throughout, which separates candidate quality from the effects of switching. When loss functions are fixed independently of selector randomness, past choices affect loss for only a bounded number of rounds, and every candidate’s own-history loss is revealed, limiting switches yields sublinear expected regret within the selected family. We also quantify the costs and additional assumptions of independent probing and deployment-only feedback. Controlled experiments show that fewer switches can either lower or raise deployed loss, depending on whether inherited histories are harmful or helpful. With Qwen3.5-9B on Spider, text-only selection has lower within-family regret than joint selection, yet produces more failures because its candidate family excludes stronger configurations.

1 Introduction

Language-model agents edit code, execute tests, and use tool feedback (Yang et al., 2024b), while recent benchmarks study learning across sequences of related tasks (Asawa et al., 2026). Consider a coding agent that handles successive tasks in a persistent workspace. Before each task, a selector chooses an instruction prompt and a model checkpoint or adapter. The agent edits code, runs tools, and receives feedback such as whether its changes pass the task’s tests. Feedback guides the next configuration choice, while the edited code and tool history remain in the workspace. The next configuration therefore inherits the consequences of earlier choices. How should we compare text-only, parameter-only, and joint adaptation in such a system?

Each opportunity to select and execute a configuration is a deployment round, indexed by tt. For example, a round can be one coding task, one question in Spider (Yu et al., 2018), or one dialogue turn in SParC (Yu et al., 2019). We consider a sequence of TT rounds, which can share state and need not be independent. The selector uses earlier feedback to choose a configuration, executes it, incurs a loss, and uses the available feedback to update future selection probabilities. Minimizing cumulative loss over these repeated choices gives an online learning problem (Cesa-Bianchi & Lugosi, 2006). Recent methods construct configurations through reflective prompt optimization (Agrawal et al., 2026), joint prompt–parameter optimization (Bo et al., 2026), and alternating harness–weight optimization (Kim et al., 2026). In our setting, candidates are constructed before evaluation. During evaluation, online learning updates their selection probabilities without constructing new prompts or adapters.

A configuration pairs reusable text, such as prompts, demonstrations, and retrieval contents, with deployable parameters, such as checkpoints or adapters (Brown et al., 2020; Lewis et al., 2020; Hu et al., 2022). Text-only selection keeps the base parameters, parameter-only selection keeps the base text, and joint selection can change both. Figure 1 illustrates these configuration families. The workspace, generated history, and tool sessions constitute operational state, which evolves even under a fixed configuration. Retaining feedback across trials can influence later behavior without changing model parameters (Shinn et al., 2023).

Our comparator is the best available joint configuration used for all TT rounds from the common initial condition, with its own resulting history. This own-history comparison follows the policy-regret perspective (Arora et al., 2012). For example, a coding agent that switches to configuration bb after using aa can encounter different code from an agent that used bb throughout.

This comparison raises three separate questions. (i) How well does the selector choose among its available candidates, when each is evaluated on the history it would have produced if used throughout? (ii) How much better is the best joint candidate than the best candidate in the selected family? (iii) Does the actual sequence of choices create a more or less favorable history than those fixed-configuration evaluations? We call the corresponding terms diagonal selection regret, family restriction, and the signed state effect. Their sum is exactly the deployed excess loss. Diagonal refers to repeating a single configuration throughout the history, and signed emphasizes that inherited state can reduce as well as increase loss.

Our strongest feedback model evaluates every candidate on its own fixed-configuration history. Ordinary deployment feedback need not supply those counterfactual losses. We also study independent probes of individual candidates and updates based only on deployed outcomes. For state-dependent guarantees, we require bounded influence: choices sufficiently far in the past no longer affect current loss, including through hidden state. These assumptions connect our analysis to online learning with memory (Anava et al., 2015). We also compare joint sampling and coordinatewise conditional selection: they agree for additive losses under a product prior, but interactions can separate their regret even when both eventually select the optimum. The online-learning methods are established (Geulen et al., 2010; Avner et al., 2012; Cheng et al., 2023). Our analysis connects their guarantees to adaptation comparators, information requirements, and signed state effects.

Controlled studies show that reducing switches helps when mixed histories are harmful and hurts when they are beneficial, even with the same per-round selection probabilities. With Qwen3.5-9B (Qwen Team, 2026) on Spider, text-only selection incurs less within-family regret than joint selection but more deployed loss because its candidates are weaker. On recursive SParC, earlier generated queries in Structured Query Language (SQL) supply the inherited state. Lazy exponential weights (EW) substantially reduces switching with only a small change in estimated expected loss.

Our main contributions are summarized as follows.

  • •

    Loss accounting. We separate selection, family restriction, and state effects relative to a common fixed joint comparator; see Section 2.

  • •

    Selection and state guarantees. We connect selection bounds to configuration families and bound expected excess loss for a selector that limits switches under exogenous losses, bounded influence, and full counterfactual feedback; see Sections 3–4.

  • •

    Weaker feedback. We quantify the costs and additional assumptions of approximate evaluation, sparse probes, and deployment-only feedback; see Section 5.

  • •

    Empirical comparisons. Controlled studies and SQL evaluations show how candidate availability and inherited state change the interpretation of selection regret and switching; see Section 6.

2 Configurations, Comparators, and Loss Decomposition

Configurations and Candidate Families.

A protocol Ξ\Xi declares the executor, available data, resource budgets, and permitted updates. An admissible configuration is one allowed and executable under these rules. Write an admissible configuration as a=(z,w)∈𝒜⊆𝒵×𝒲a=(z,w)\in\mathcal{A}\subseteq\mathcal{Z}\times\mathcal{W}, where zz is reusable text and ww specifies deployable parameters. Learned continuous prompt tensors also belong to ww. Relative to a base pair (z0,w0)(z_{0},w_{0}), the text-only family 𝒜Z=𝒜∩(𝒵×{w0})\mathcal{A}_{Z}=\mathcal{A}\cap(\mathcal{Z}\times\{w_{0}\}) holds parameters fixed. The parameter-only family 𝒜W=𝒜∩({z0}×𝒲)\mathcal{A}_{W}=\mathcal{A}\cap(\{z_{0}\}\times\mathcal{W}) holds text fixed. Their union is 𝒜∪=𝒜Z∪𝒜W\mathcal{A}_{\cup}=\mathcal{A}_{Z}\cup\mathcal{A}_{W}, while the joint family is 𝒜Z​W=𝒜\mathcal{A}_{ZW}=\mathcal{A}. We select from finite candidates 𝒞Z​W⊆𝒜\mathcal{C}_{ZW}\subseteq\mathcal{A} constructed before evaluation and containing the base pair, with 𝒞e=𝒞Z​W∩𝒜e\mathcal{C}_{e}=\mathcal{C}_{ZW}\cap\mathcal{A}_{e} for e∈{Z,W,∪,ZW}e\in\{Z,W,\cup,ZW\}.

One Deployment Round.

At round t∈{1,2,…,T}t\in\{1,2,\ldots,T\}, the selector chooses At∈𝒞eA_{t}\in\mathcal{C}_{e} using the feedback available from earlier rounds. The executor applies AtA_{t} to task input xtx_{t} in operational state sts_{t}, producing outputs and tool actions, incurring a normalized loss ℓt∈[0,1]\ell_{t}\in[0,1], and advancing the state to st+1s_{t+1}. Loss can indicate task failure, while state can retain generated code or dialogue history. The permitted feedback updates future selection probabilities, while execution changes the operational state. Incurring a loss does not imply observing every candidate’s loss. The formal executor and state transition are provided in Appendix A.1.

Fixed-Configuration Histories and Feedback.

Fix a common initial condition and an exogenous random tape, independent of selector randomness, determining losses Ft(a1:t)∈[0,1]F_{t}(a_{1:t})\in[0,1] for histories a1:t=(a1,…,at)a_{1:t}=(a_{1},\ldots,a_{t}). For the deployed history, ℓt=Ft(A1:t)\ell_{t}=F_{t}(A_{1:t}). Each alternative history reruns the state and any deployment-responsive tasks. The diagonal loss of a fixed configuration aa is

dt​(a)=Ft​(a,…,a).d_{t}(a)=F_{t}(a,\ldots,a). (1)

This is its round-tt loss if it had been used from the beginning. After switching from aa to bb, for example, the round-two deployed loss is F2​(a,b)F_{2}(a,b), whereas the diagonal loss of the current choice is d2​(b)=F2​(b,b)d_{2}(b)=F_{2}(b,b). Full diagonal feedback reveals every dt​(a)d_{t}(a) after round tt, sparse feedback probes individual candidates independently of deployment, and deployment-only feedback reveals the realized loss ℓt\ell_{t}. The accounting identity requires no observation of counterfactual losses, while the learning guarantees state their feedback assumptions separately.

Comparator and Loss Accounting.

Let DT​(a)=∑t=1Tdt​(a)D_{T}(a)=\sum_{t=1}^{T}d_{t}(a) be the cumulative loss of using aa throughout. The best fixed value within family ee is VT,𝒞e=mina∈𝒞e⁡DT​(a)V_{T,\mathcal{C}}^{e}=\min_{a\in\mathcal{C}_{e}}D_{T}(a). Our common comparator has value VT,𝒞Z​WV_{T,\mathcal{C}}^{ZW}: hindsight selects one joint candidate for the entire horizon, with its own induced history. Write LTdep=∑t=1TFt(A1:t)L_{T}^{\mathrm{dep}}=\sum_{t=1}^{T}F_{t}(A_{1:t}) for the learner’s cumulative deployed loss and LTdiag=∑t=1Tdt​(At)L_{T}^{\mathrm{diag}}=\sum_{t=1}^{T}d_{t}(A_{t}) for its choices evaluated on their respective fixed-configuration histories. The latter sum need not describe one deployment trajectory. Adding and subtracting it and the best within-family value gives the decomposition.

Proposition 1 (Selection, restriction, and state accounting).

For every trajectory with At∈𝒞eA_{t}\in\mathcal{C}_{e},

LTdep−VT,𝒞Z​W=LTdiag−VT,𝒞e⏟diagonal selection+VT,𝒞e−VT,𝒞Z​W⏟family restriction+LTdep−LTdiag⏟signed state effect.L_{T}^{\mathrm{dep}}-V_{T,\mathcal{C}}^{ZW}=\underbrace{L_{T}^{\mathrm{diag}}-V_{T,\mathcal{C}}^{e}}_{\text{diagonal selection}}+\underbrace{V_{T,\mathcal{C}}^{e}-V_{T,\mathcal{C}}^{ZW}}_{\text{family restriction}}+\underbrace{L_{T}^{\mathrm{dep}}-L_{T}^{\mathrm{diag}}}_{\text{signed state effect}}. (2)

Only family restriction is necessarily nonnegative; the identity also holds in expectation.

Selection compares choices within the available family, restriction charges its gap to the joint family, and state accounts for the actual history’s benefit or harm. Stateless systems have zero state effect. For fixed diagonal tables, identical action marginals give equal expected diagonal loss, while different deployment histories can help or hurt. Appendix A.1.2 details sampling residuals and comparator averaging. The proofs appear in Appendix B.

3 Selection and Family Restriction

Selection and Prior Complexity.

4 State Effects and Policy Regret

Policy regret groups selection and state in (2): RTpol​(Q)=𝔼​LTdep−𝔼​∫DT​(a)​𝑑Q​(a)R_{T}^{\mathrm{pol}}(Q)=\mathbb{E}L_{T}^{\mathrm{dep}}-\mathbb{E}\int D_{T}(a)\,\mathrm{d}Q(a), where the comparator draws once from QQ and deploys it from the common initial condition (Arora et al., 2012). Point regret takes Q=δaQ=\delta_{a}. Evaluating comparators on the learner’s realized state instead gives external regret.

Proposition 5 (Zero external regret and linear policy regret).

A deterministic two-configuration persistent-state system admits a trajectory with zero realized-state external regret and policy regret T−1T-1 against a fixed configuration.

Proposition 6 (Linear policy regret).

For every optimizer whose first action uses only common pre-round history and private coins, and every T≥2T\geq 2, some deterministic two-configuration environment gives expected policy regret at least (T−1)/2(T-1)/2, when its index and transition kernel are unknown before that action.

Assumption 1 (Component-specific bounded influence).

For integers mZ,mW≥0m_{Z},m_{W}\geq 0, measurable functions ftf_{t}, fixed before learner randomization, give loss ft(zmax⁡{1,t−mZ}:t;wmax⁡{1,t−mW}:t)∈[0,1]f_{t}(z_{\max\{1,t-m_{Z}\}:t};w_{\max\{1,t-m_{W}\}:t})\in[0,1]. Older coordinates have no influence, including through hidden state, while interactions within the windows are unrestricted.

Put m=mmax=max⁡{mZ,mW}m=m_{\max}=\max\{m_{Z},m_{W}\}, truncating horizons at T−1T-1. The diagonal dt​(z,w)d_{t}(z,w) repeats each coordinate throughout its window. Influence measures persistence after replacement.

Assumption 2 (Diagonal counterfactual evaluation oracle).

After round tt, every own-trajectory loss dt​(a)d_{t}(a), a∈𝒜a\in\mathcal{A}, is revealed.

Lazy Exponential Weights.

Apply the EW update from Section 3 to dtd_{t}, starting with q1=μq_{1}=\mu and A1∼μA_{1}\sim\mu. After round t<Tt<T, retain AtA_{t} with probability e−η​dt​(At)e^{-\eta d_{t}(A_{t})} and otherwise refresh from qt+1q_{t+1} (Geulen et al., 2010; Kalai & Vempala, 2005). Refreshes preserve At∼qtA_{t}\sim q_{t} and occur at most η⁡(T−1)\eta(T-1) times in expectation. Each refresh contaminates at most mm rounds. This requires own-trajectory evaluation.

Proposition 7 (Matched marginals isolate state effects).

For fixed exogenous losses, family, prior, and learning rate, independent and lazy draws with the same diagonal feedback and EW marginals have equal expected diagonal losses. Hence,

𝔼​LTdep,lazy−𝔼​LTdep,ind=𝔼⁡[LTdep,lazy−LTdiag,lazy]−𝔼⁡[LTdep,ind−LTdiag,ind].\mathbb{E}L_{T}^{\mathrm{dep,lazy}}-\mathbb{E}L_{T}^{\mathrm{dep,ind}}=\mathbb{E}[L_{T}^{\mathrm{dep,lazy}}-L_{T}^{\mathrm{diag,lazy}}]-\mathbb{E}[L_{T}^{\mathrm{dep,ind}}-L_{T}^{\mathrm{diag,ind}}]. (10)

Thus fewer switches can help or hurt. The identity also holds conditional on shared exogenous approximate feedback.

Theorem 2 (Lazy policy regret under bounded influence).

Under Assumptions 1–2, for every η>0\eta>0 and Q≪μQ\ll\mu with finite CQ=KL(Q∥μ)C_{Q}=\operatorname{KL}(Q\,\|\,\mu),

RTpol​(Q)≤CQ/η+η⁡[T/8+mmax​(T−1)].R_{T}^{\mathrm{pol}}(Q)\leq C_{Q}/\eta+\eta\left[T/8+m_{\max}(T-1)\right]. (11)

For CQ>0C_{Q}>0, comparator-dependent tuning gives the following:

η⋆\displaystyle\eta^{\star} =CQ/(T/8+mmax​(T−1)),\displaystyle=\sqrt{C_{Q}/(T/8+m_{\max}(T-1))}, (12)
RTpol​(Q)\displaystyle R_{T}^{\mathrm{pol}}(Q) ≤2​CQ[T/+mmax(T−1)]≤2​T​CQ​(mmax+1/8)=O⁡((+mmax)​T​CQ).\displaystyle\!\leq\!2\sqrt{C_{Q}[T/8\!+\!m_{\max}(T\!-\!1)]}\!\leq\!2\sqrt{TC_{Q}(m_{\max}\!+\!1/8)}\!=\!O\!\left(\!\!\sqrt{(1\!+\!m_{\max})TC_{Q}}\right). (13)

For CQ=0C_{Q}=0, draw once from μ\mu without refreshing; regret is zero.

The m​η​(T−1)m\eta(T-1) term controls state, while the remaining terms control selection. These established low-switch methods (Geulen et al., 2010; Anava et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2022) connect prior complexity to influence. Uniform priors give CQ=log⁡KC_{Q}=\log K for every point comparator.

Proposition 8 (Mode-restricted lazy influence rates).

Under Assumptions 1–2, run lazy EW with priors μZ=π⊗δw0\mu_{Z}=\pi\otimes\delta_{w_{0}} and μW=δz0⊗ρ\mu_{W}=\delta_{z_{0}}\otimes\rho, supported on 𝒜Z\mathcal{A}_{Z} and 𝒜W\mathcal{A}_{W}, respectively. For fixed comparators QZ≪πQ_{Z}\ll\pi and QW≪ρQ_{W}\ll\rho, let CZ=KL(QZ∥π)C_{Z}=\operatorname{KL}(Q_{Z}\,\|\,\pi) and CW=KL(QW∥ρ)C_{W}=\operatorname{KL}(Q_{W}\,\|\,\rho) be finite. For every η>0\eta>0, text-only and parameter-only selection satisfy

RTpol​(QZ⊗δw0)\displaystyle R_{T}^{\mathrm{pol}}(Q_{Z}\otimes\delta_{w_{0}}) ≤CZ/η+η⁡[T/8+mZ​(T−1)],\displaystyle\leq C_{Z}/\eta+\eta[T/8+m_{Z}(T-1)], (14)
RTpol​(δz0⊗QW)\displaystyle R_{T}^{\mathrm{pol}}(\delta_{z_{0}}\otimes Q_{W}) ≤CW/η+η⁡[T/8+mW​(T−1)].\displaystyle\leq C_{W}/\eta+\eta[T/8+m_{W}(T-1)]. (15)

Freezing one coordinate removes its switching contribution: the state charge depends on the influence horizon of the coordinate being changed. For positive complexity, comparator-tuned rates are O⁡((1+mZ)​T​CZ)O(\sqrt{(1+m_{Z})TC_{Z}}) and O⁡((1+mW)​T​CW)O(\sqrt{(1+m_{W})TC_{W}}). For the best fixed candidate within each finite family, add family restriction to compare with the joint optimum. Different upper bounds alone do not establish which mode performs better. Appendix A.3.2 gives localization and coupling details, while Appendix A.3.3 treats whole-policy selection across reset episodes. Proofs are in Appendix B.3.

5 Feedback Requirements and Extensions

Counterfactual feedback evaluates each candidate on the history it would have produced if used throughout. Deployment feedback reports only the loss actually incurred. We now quantify what changes as feedback becomes less informative. Fix a finite family 𝒞\mathcal{C} of KK candidates with positive prior μ\mu, and a comparator distribution QQ fixed independently of learner and probe randomness. Write m=mmaxm=m_{\max} and CQ=KL(Q∥μ)C_{Q}=\operatorname{KL}(Q\,\|\,\mu) as in Section 4.

Approximate Full Counterfactual Feedback.

Theorem 2 assumes exact diagonal losses. An exogenous full estimate sequence in [0,1][0,1] with uniform round-tt error ϵt\epsilon_{t} adds at most 2​∑tϵt2\sum_{t}\epsilon_{t} to its bound. Conditionally unbiased estimates in the same range preserve the expected bound; refer to Appendix A.4.1. The entire evaluator must be independent of deployment randomness. Even a common estimation offset can alter retention and state effects while leaving EW marginals unchanged.

Sparse Independent Probes.

Under the bounded-influence condition in Assumption 1, an autonomous evaluator can instead probe one candidate Jt∼qtJ_{t}\sim q_{t} after each round. Its outcome Zt∈[0,1]Z_{t}\in[0,1] must have conditional mean dt​(Jt)d_{t}(J_{t}) given the exogenous response tree, earlier evaluation history, and JtJ_{t}. Conditional on that tree, the entire evaluator is independent of deployment randomness, consumes no deployed actions or outcomes, and is unchanged by deployment interventions. Probing also leaves the tree unchanged; see Assumption 3. Initialize q1=μq_{1}=\mu and A1∼μA_{1}\sim\mu, and update EW using d^t(a)=𝟏{Jt=a}Zt/qt(a)\widehat{d}_{t}(a)=\mathbf{1}\{J_{t}=a\}Z_{t}/q_{t}(a). Retain AtA_{t} with probability e−η​d^t​(At)e^{-\eta\widehat{d}_{t}(A_{t})} and otherwise refresh from qt+1q_{t+1} using independent deployment randomness.

Theorem 3 (Sparse-diagonal policy regret).

Under Assumption 3, with probe law rt=qtr_{t}=q_{t}, every fixed QQ and η>0\eta>0 satisfy the following:

RTpol​(Q)≤CQ/η+η⁡[K​T/2+m⁡(T−1)].R_{T}^{\mathrm{pol}}(Q)\leq C_{Q}/\eta+\eta\left[KT/2+m(T-1)\right]. (16)

For CQ>0C_{Q}>0, η=CQ/[K​T/2+m⁡(T−1)]\eta=\sqrt{C_{Q}/[KT/2+m(T-1)]} gives

RTpol​(Q)≤2​CQ​[K​T/2+m⁡(T−1)].R_{T}^{\mathrm{pol}}(Q)\leq 2\sqrt{C_{Q}[KT/2+m(T-1)]}. (17)

For CQ=0C_{Q}=0, drawing once from μ\mu gives zero expected regret.

One probe per round reduces K​TKT counterfactual evaluations to TT probes, replacing the full-feedback selection term η​T/8\eta T/8 by η​K​T/2\eta KT/2 while preserving the state term. Simulation or cloning costs remain, and independence from only the current deployment draw is insufficient. Appendix A.4.5 gives the formal process and refined bounds.

Deployment-Only Feedback.

Without a counterfactual evaluator, hold each chosen configuration for a block of bb rounds, where 1≤b≤T1\leq b\leq T is an integer. There are J=⌊T/b⌋J=\lfloor T/b\rfloor complete blocks and r=T−b​Jr=T-bJ remaining rounds. Block jj starts at sj=(j−1)​b+1s_{j}=(j-1)b+1 after the realized prefix Hj=A1:sj−1H_{j}=A_{1:s_{j}-1}. We write UU explicitly for the external random tape introduced in Section 2.

Definition 1 (Block counterfactual).

The average loss from repeating aa after the actual prefix, rerunning environmental responses, is

gj​(a)=(1/b)​∑u=1bFsj+u−1​(Hj,au,U),g_{j}(a)=(1/b)\sum_{u=1}^{b}F_{s_{j}+u-1}(H_{j},a^{u};U), (18)

where aua^{u} denotes uu repetitions of aa.

Starting from p1=μp_{1}=\mu, deploy a fresh private draw Bj∼pjB_{j}\sim p_{j} throughout block jj and update EW using g^j(a)=𝟏{Bj=a}Zj/pj(a)\widehat{g}_{j}(a)=\mathbf{1}\{B_{j}=a\}Z_{j}/p_{j}(a), where Zj=gj​(Bj)Z_{j}=g_{j}(B_{j}) is the observed block-average loss. Retain the last configuration for the remaining rr rounds. The signed causal reaction compares repeating a comparator after the learner’s prefixes with using it from the beginning, over the complete blocks:

Γb​(Q)=𝔼​∑a∈𝒞Q⁡(a)​[b​∑j=1Jgj​(a)−∑t=1b​Jdt​(a)].\Gamma_{b}(Q)=\mathbb{E}\sum_{a\in\mathcal{C}}Q(a)\left[b\sum_{j=1}^{J}g_{j}(a)-\sum_{t=1}^{bJ}d_{t}(a)\right]. (19)

It includes changes in tasks, user responses, and operational state.

Theorem 4 (Oracle-free causal policy-regret inequality).

For causal responses Ft∈[0,1]F_{t}\in[0,1] driven by an external tape independent of private learner coins, the block algorithm satisfies, for every fixed QQ and η>0\eta>0,

RTpol​(Q)≤b​CQ/η+η​b​K​J/2+Γb​(Q)+r.R_{T}^{\mathrm{pol}}(Q)\leq bC_{Q}/\eta+\eta bKJ/2+\Gamma_{b}(Q)+r. (20)

No oracle for gjg_{j}, dtd_{t}, or Γb\Gamma_{b} is required.

The first two terms bound selection from observed block losses, while Γb​(Q)\Gamma_{b}(Q) accounts for the different histories and rr covers the unfinished block. This retains the causal discrepancy in policy-regret mini-batching (Arora et al., 2012), and uncontrolled reaction can remain linear. If the complete causal system has influence horizon mm, including task selection and evaluation, then |Γb​(Q)|≤min⁡{m,b}​(J−1)|\Gamma_{b}(Q)|\leq\min\{m,b\}(J-1): only the first mm rounds of each later block can remember its prefix. Optimizing bb and η\eta yields O⁡((m​K​CQ)1/3​T2/3)O((mKC_{Q})^{1/3}T^{2/3}) for fixed positive m,K,CQm,K,C_{Q} and sufficiently large TT; see Corollary 12. Use b=1b=1 for m=0m=0, and a single prior draw for CQ=0C_{Q}=0. Forgetting in a cache alone does not establish this complete-system condition.

For random response trees, independence and unbiasedness must hold conditionally to compare with the tree’s best fixed candidate. Query-adaptive autonomous evaluation supports fixed or best expected-loss comparators, not comparators selected using probe noise. Appendix A.4 provides supporting lemmas and extensions.

6 Empirical Analysis

Experimental Setup.

Controlled studies isolate selection, family restriction, and signed state effects on deployed loss. SQL experiments use Qwen3.5-9B (Qwen Team, 2026) on Spider (Yu et al., 2018) and SParC (Yu et al., 2019). Excess loss is measured relative to each table’s or benchmark’s best fixed joint configuration unless a paired contrast is specified. Summaries and error bars use means ±\pm one standard error (SE). Refer to Appendices C and C.1 for detailed designs, numerical results, and uncertainty.

Joint and Coordinatewise Selection.

Joint EW and text-then-parameter sweeps share the uniform prior, preceding loss rows, and rate schedule on the additive and barrier tables of Section 3. Family restriction, state effects, and the best fixed loss are zero, so cumulative loss equals regret. The additive control gives equal regret, whereas one coordinatewise sweep incurs substantially more regret on the barrier under both schedules, as in Figure 3. Under the slow schedule, high final-round optimal-selection probability coexists with this accumulated gap. Extra sweeps reduce the gap at additional computation cost without new feedback; see Figure 8 and Appendix C.2 for details.

Selection and Signed State Effects.

Fixed-advantage, changing-quality, and no-signal diagonal tables use ft=dt​(At)+λ​Itf_{t}=d_{t}(A_{t})+\lambda I_{t}, where ItI_{t} indicates mixed configurations in the relevant coordinate histories. Negative, zero, and positive λ\lambda give beneficial, neutral, and harmful state effects. State and approximate-feedback figures use (mZ,mW)=(4,0)(m_{Z},m_{W})=(4,0); see Appendix C.3 for details. Independent and lazy EW have identical expected diagonal losses, as presented in Figure 9, but lazy EW has lower deployed loss under harmful state and higher loss under beneficial state; see Figure 4. Fewer switches can therefore help or hurt. Without a selection signal, draw-once has zero excess while both EW selectors incur harmful state costs, as shown in Figure 10.

Feedback Accuracy, Switching, and Evaluation Cost.

We perturb diagonal feedback at T=4,096T=4{,}096, fixing the true table, prior, rate, and learner random inputs. A common offset preserves selection distributions but changes ordinary lazy EW’s switching and state costs, while the trajectories of independent EW and centered lazy EW remain unchanged. A reference-opposing bias changes both selection and state, as shown in Figure 3; refer to Appendix C.4 for experimental details and additional results. Increasing the Bernoulli sampling budget reduces feedback error without monotone deployed-loss improvement in the displayed conditions; see Figure 12.

Restricted Feedback on Controlled Losses.

On the four-candidate joint family, we compare full-diagonal and one-probe lazy EW, deployment-only EW with blocks b∈{1,2,4,8,16}b\in\{1,2,4,8,16\}, and draw-once. All use uniform priors and regime-specific rates, so both information and learning rate vary; refer to Appendix C.5. At T=1,024T=1{,}024 and mZ=mW=4m_{Z}=m_{W}=4, increasing bb from 1 to 16 lowers excess under harmful state but raises it under beneficial state, as shown in Figure 6. These results illustrate how blocks sacrifice updates and suppress both kinds of state effects. Negative excess means a changing history beats every fixed configuration under this synthetic law.

Selection and Family Restriction on Spider.

Spider compares text, parameter, union, and joint families with 6, 4, 9, and 24 configurations against each seed’s best fixed joint candidate. Full-diagonal EW uses a fixed question order and a uniform prior. Independent and lazy expectations coincide because state is absent; refer to Appendices C.6 and C.7 for details. Text EW has lower selection regret than joint EW, but its larger family restriction produces higher expected deployed loss, as shown in Figure 65(c). Joint EW also has lower mean loss than parameter EW. Averaging all base-anchored K=4K=4 subsets gives similar parameter and joint excess losses, as presented in Figure 65(d). The full-pool ordering therefore need not survive equal candidate counts. Demonstrations also show stronger mean improvement beyond additive prompt–adapter effects than verification, as presented in Figure 77(a); refer to Appendix C.7 for details.

State Effects on SParC.

SParC isolates history effects under matched configuration marginals. Recursive history retains earlier generated SQL, while cleared history removes it, retaining the schema and raw utterances. Dialogue resets bound influence by four rounds. Both couplings share diagonal losses and an influence-dependent rate, which is retained in the cleared control. Mixed-history outcomes measure state effects without updating selection; see Appendix C.8. Independent EW has lower estimated recursive-history loss despite identical expected diagonal loss, as shown in Figure 77(b). Lazy EW substantially reduces switching with only a small change in estimated expected loss; see Table 7. Fewer mixed histories remove both beneficial and harmful effects. These data do not establish that fewer switches worsen performance. Clearing eliminates state effects and equalizes expected deployed losses but changes the diagonal table and comparator, so cross-condition totals cannot identify state effects.

Restricted Feedback on Precomputed SQL Losses.

We apply the controlled feedback regimes to precomputed Spider and cleared-SParC loss matrices, keeping outcomes, order, prior, and joint comparator fixed. We use zero-influence learning rates; see Appendix C.9. Full feedback has the lowest mean excess on both tasks, whereas one-probe feedback queries fewer diagonal entries but incurs more excess, as presented in Figures 77(c) and 77(d). One-probe and deployment-only b=1b=1 means are close; refer to Appendix C.9. The longest blocks reduce switches but raise mean excess relative to b=1b=1 on both tasks; see Table 8.

7 Related Work

Parameter Adaptation and Model Editing.

Weight adaptation includes full tuning, adapters, low-rank updates (Houlsby et al., 2019; Hu et al., 2022), continuous prompt/prefix tuning (Li & Liang, 2021; Lester et al., 2021), and targeted editing (Meng et al., 2022). Updates can cause interference and forgetting (Kirkpatrick et al., 2017), with low-rank and full tuning differing even at similar performance (Shuttleworth et al., 2025). Comparisons with in-context learning report task-dependent accuracy, generalization, and cost tradeoffs (Liu et al., 2022; Mosbach et al., 2023; Ghosh et al., 2026; Razumovskaia et al., 2025), while theory characterizes when prompting can match weight tuning (Genewein et al., 2025). Joint construction includes BetterTogether (Soylu et al., 2024), MetaTuner (Bo et al., 2026), fast–slow updates (Tiwari et al., 2026), and WHALE’s alternation of online rejection-sampling tuning with Meta-Harness search (Kim et al., 2026). Our conditional sampler studies selection within a fixed family, with candidate construction.

Expert Advice, Mixture Priors, and Limited Switching.

Hedge and external regret compare fixed experts (Hannan, 1957; Foster & Vohra, 1999; Littlestone & Warmuth, 1994; Freund & Schapire, 1997; Cesa-Bianchi & Lugosi, 2006), and KL change-of-measure extends the analysis to measurable priors. Bandit, tracking, and sleeping/growing-expert models change feedback, comparators, or availability (Auer et al., 2002; Bubeck & Cesa-Bianchi, 2012; Herbster & Warmuth, 1998; Cortes et al., 2019; Mourtada & Maillard, 2017). Lazy and limited-switch methods control regret and action changes (Kalai & Vempala, 2005; Geulen et al., 2010; Altschuler & Talwar, 2018). Switching costs admit T\sqrt{T} full-information and Θ~​(T2/3)\widetilde{\Theta}(T^{2/3}) adversarial-bandit rates; bounded-memory adversaries can force T2/3T^{2/3} under ordinary full information (Cesa-Bianchi et al., 2013; Dekel et al., 2014). Zhang et al. (2022) combine prior divergence and movement penalties in comparator-adaptive finite-expert bounds. Under exogenous losses, coupling converts marginal movement into expected switches.

Appendix E provides additional related work.

8 Conclusion

We decomposed deployed loss over the best fixed joint configuration into selection, family restriction, and signed state effects. Low regret within a candidate family, eventual optimal selection, and infrequent switching can each occur alongside higher cumulative loss. Under the stated influence and feedback assumptions, EW with infrequent switching bounds selection regret and state effects, while weaker feedback introduces additional costs and requires further assumptions. Our controlled and SQL experiments illustrate how these distinctions arise within the evaluated candidate families.

AI use statement

We used GPT-5.6 Sol (OpenAI, 2026a) and GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI, 2026b) as our primary generative AI models. We used these models to refine research ideas, derive mathematical proofs, implement experiments, and draft and polish the manuscript. The human authors take responsibility for the final content of this work, including all claims, proofs, experimental results, code, and text produced with AI assistance.

Ethics statement

We do not identify direct ethical concerns arising from the theoretical analysis and benchmark experiments presented in this work. However, methods for adapting language-model systems could be used in applications with harmful consequences. We acknowledge this potential and emphasize the importance of responsible use and appropriate safeguards.

Appendix A Supplementary Theory

This appendix supplies the detailed setup, exact constants, supporting statements, and extensions for Sections 2–5. Proofs of the main and supplementary results appear in Appendix B.

A.1 Configurations, Comparators, and Loss Decomposition

This section describes the configuration spaces, admissible families, and execution traces used to define the loss decomposition in (2).

A.1.1 Admissible Configurations and Execution

Let θ0\theta_{0} denote the base model. The admissible configuration families depend on how updates are produced and deployed.

Definition 2 (Adaptation protocol and admissible families).

An adaptation protocol Ξ\Xi declares the base model, executor and interfaces, available data, resource budgets, and permitted text- and parameter-update procedures. It induces standard Borel spaces (𝒵Ξ,ℱ𝒵)(\mathcal{Z}_{\Xi},\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{Z}}) and (𝒲Ξ,ℱ𝒲)(\mathcal{W}_{\Xi},\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{W}}) of admissible text and parameter configurations, together with a measurable compatibility family 𝒜Ξ⊆𝒵Ξ×𝒲Ξ\mathcal{A}_{\Xi}\subseteq\mathcal{Z}_{\Xi}\times\mathcal{W}_{\Xi} of deployed pairs containing the base pair. Cross-mode simulation is admissible only if Ξ\Xi permits and charges its interfaces, storage, and computation.

Fix Ξ\Xi and suppress its subscript. We specify evaluator and feedback assumptions separately. Standard-Borel spaces accommodate finite, countable, and usual continuous configurations. The text configuration zz, with base object z0z_{0}, comprises reusable objects with canonical token serializations: prompts, retained memory, demonstrations, retrieval contents, and harness instructions. Literal serializations are countable, while continuous relaxations require a Ξ\Xi-declared quantizer or serializer for deployment evaluation.

A parameter configuration w∈𝒲w\in\mathcal{W} specifies model parameters θ⁡(w)\theta(w), including learned auxiliary tensors, with θ⁡(w0)=θ0\theta(w_{0})=\theta_{0}. It may be continuous or atomic, including checkpoints, adapters, patches, and learned prompt/prefix tensors. In particular, dense tensors belong to ww. The measurable executor exec\operatorname{exec} combines (z,θ⁡(w))(z,\theta(w)), task input, and possibly persistent operational state ss: environment state, tool sessions, caches, and runtime objects not selected as reusable configuration.

For a current configuration a=(z,w)a=(z,w), define the admissible one-coordinate update sets:

𝒰Z​(a)\displaystyle\mathcal{U}_{Z}(a) =𝒜∩(𝒵×{w}),\displaystyle=\mathcal{A}\cap(\mathcal{Z}\times\{w\}), (21)
𝒰W​(a)\displaystyle\mathcal{U}_{W}(a) =𝒜∩({z}×𝒲).\displaystyle=\mathcal{A}\cap(\{z\}\times\mathcal{W}). (22)

These updates hold the other coordinate at its current value, whereas joint updates select from 𝒜\mathcal{A}. The comparison families in Section 2 instead fix coordinates at the base pair a0=(z0,w0)a_{0}=(z_{0},w_{0}). For non-Cartesian compatibility families, priors must be supported on 𝒜\mathcal{A}. The prior-based results remain valid, but product KL identities need not hold. Joint configurations may change both base coordinates regardless of installation order.

Given task input xtx_{t} at round tt, execution produces a trace, loss, and next state:

τt\displaystyle\tau_{t} ∼exec⁡(Mθ⁡(wt),zt,st,xt),\displaystyle\sim\operatorname{exec}(M_{\theta(w_{t})},z_{t},s_{t},x_{t}), (23)
ℓt\displaystyle\ell_{t} =ℓ⁡(xt,τt)∈[0,1],\displaystyle=\ell(x_{t},\tau_{t})\in[0,1], (24)
st+1\displaystyle s_{t+1} ∼Pt(⋅∣st,zt,wt,xt,τt).\displaystyle\sim P_{t}(\cdot\mid s_{t},z_{t},w_{t},x_{t},\tau_{t}). (25)

Here τt\tau_{t} records outputs and intermediate actions, and PtP_{t} governs state transitions. The normalized loss may combine quality and per-use resources. Appendix D treats installation and path-dependent transition costs separately.

A.1.2 Fixed Comparators and Loss Decomposition

We use the candidate families, causal losses, and cumulative comparator values defined in Section 2. Exogenous tasks are shared across counterfactual histories, while deployment-responsive tasks, users, and environments are rerun under each history. The accounting identity (2) conditions on this response tree. We refine its restriction and averaging conventions below. For text-only or parameter-only selection, restriction can be further split at the union family into VT,𝒞e−VT,𝒞∪V_{T,\mathcal{C}}^{e}-V_{T,\mathcal{C}}^{\cup} and VT,𝒞∪−VT,𝒞Z​WV_{T,\mathcal{C}}^{\cup}-V_{T,\mathcal{C}}^{ZW}. Neither difference alone measures a nonadditive text–parameter interaction.

For fixed diagonal tables and action marginals qtq_{t}, 𝔼​LTdiag=∑t∫dt​d​qt\mathbb{E}L_{T}^{\mathrm{diag}}=\sum_{t}\int d_{t}\,\mathrm{d}q_{t}. Substituting this expectation into a realized trajectory’s decomposition requires the sampling residual:

LTdiag−𝔼​LTdiag.L_{T}^{\mathrm{diag}}-\mathbb{E}L_{T}^{\mathrm{diag}}. (26)

Experiments retain this residual and distinguish averaged hindsight optima from expected-loss optima: generally, 𝔼​mina​DT​(a)≠mina⁡𝔼​DT​(a)\mathbb{E}\min_{a}D_{T}(a)\neq\min_{a}\mathbb{E}D_{T}(a).

A.1.3 Feasibility and Configuration Reachability

Feasibility asks whether a requested operational effect is attainable, separately from its loss.

Definition 3 (Protocol-relative update reachability).

Fix an operating condition c=(t,s,x)c=(t,s,x). For configuration b=(z′,w′)b=(z^{\prime},w^{\prime}), let Γc​(b)\Gamma_{c}(b) be the law of the execution trace and next state (τ,s+)(\tau,s^{+}) obtained by executing Mθ⁡(w′)M_{\theta(w^{\prime})} with z′z^{\prime} from (s,x)(s,x) and applying PtP_{t}. From current configuration aa, the reachable sets are

ℜZ​(c,a)\displaystyle\mathfrak{R}_{Z}(c;a) ={Γc​(b):b∈𝒰Z​(a)},\displaystyle=\{\Gamma_{c}(b):b\in\mathcal{U}_{Z}(a)\}, (27)
ℜW​(c,a)\displaystyle\mathfrak{R}_{W}(c;a) ={Γc​(b):b∈𝒰W​(a)}.\displaystyle=\{\Gamma_{c}(b):b\in\mathcal{U}_{W}(a)\}. (28)

A target effect is feasible for a mode when its law belongs to that mode’s reachable set, while a task-specific discrepancy defines approximate feasibility.

Two updates have the same effect at cc when their trace/state laws agree, while approximate feasibility uses a declared discrepancy tolerance. Neither reachable set need contain the other, and both depend on Ξ\Xi and potentially cc. Finite search failure does not prove nonreachability, and budget-violating effects are inadmissible. For multi-round targets, replace Γc\Gamma_{c} by the declared policy’s rollout law.

These definitions imply neither disjoint neural effects nor persistence determined by artifact type.

A.2 Selection and Family Restriction

We bound stateless full-information selection in (2), then distinguish restriction, coordinatewise selection, and candidate discovery.

A.2.1 Finite Candidate Selection

Section 3 states the finite-family update (3) and selection-plus-restriction bound (6). The proof is in Appendix B.2. With a uniform prior over Ne>1N_{e}>1 candidates, choosing η=8​log⁡Ne/T\eta=\sqrt{8\log N_{e}/T} bounds selection regret by T​log⁡Ne/2\sqrt{T\log N_{e}/2} without knowing the best candidate. Restriction can remain linear, although expanding a family can reduce it while increasing selection complexity, independently of the mode label. A singleton family incurs no diagonal selection regret.

A.2.2 Measurable Priors and Comparator Complexity

To include continuous parameters, let (𝒜,ℱ𝒜)(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{A}}) be a standard-Borel space, not necessarily a product, with prior μ\mu fixed before the losses. Deployment of a=(z,w)a=(z,w) has measurable expected loss

Lt​(a)=Lt​(z,w)=𝔼τ∼exec⁡(Mθ⁡(w),z,xt)​[ℓ⁡(xt,τ)]∈[0,1].L_{t}(a)=L_{t}(z,w)=\mathbb{E}_{\tau\sim\operatorname{exec}(M_{\theta(w)},z,x_{t})}[\ell(x_{t},\tau)]\in[0,1]. (29)

This evaluator averages model, tool, and harness randomness in (24), whereas Section 2 fixes exogenous randomness. The bounds apply to either table under its comparator averaging convention.

Loss LtL_{t} may depend on earlier history but is fixed before at∼pta_{t}\sim p_{t}. The learner incurs Lt​(at)L_{t}(a_{t}) and observes all of LtL_{t}. Given pre-draw information ℋt−1\mathcal{H}_{t-1}, its conditional mean loss is

L¯t=𝔼⁡[Lt​(at)∣ℋt−1]=∫𝒜Lt​(a)​d​pt​(a).\overline{L}_{t}=\mathbb{E}[L_{t}(a_{t})\mid\mathcal{H}_{t-1}]=\int_{\mathcal{A}}L_{t}(a)\,\mathrm{d}p_{t}(a). (30)

Averaging over the learner’s draw defines conditional pseudo-regret, and an outer expectation gives expected pseudo-regret.

Definition 4 (Point and distributional external regret).

For a fixed reference configuration a⋆∈𝒜a^{\star}\in\mathcal{A}, define

RT​(a⋆)=∑t=1TL¯t−∑t=1TLt​(a⋆).R_{T}(a^{\star})=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\overline{L}_{t}-\sum_{t=1}^{T}L_{t}(a^{\star}). (31)

For a fixed probability measure QQ on 𝒜\mathcal{A}, define

RT​(Q)=∑t=1TL¯t−∑t=1T∫𝒜Lt​(a)​𝑑Q​(a).R_{T}(Q)=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\overline{L}_{t}-\sum_{t=1}^{T}\int_{\mathcal{A}}L_{t}(a)\,\mathrm{d}Q(a). (32)

The comparator holds one draw from fixed QQ throughout the sequence, with RT​(a⋆)=RT​(δa⋆)R_{T}(a^{\star})=R_{T}(\delta_{a^{\star}}). Overall point regret is

RText=supa⋆∈𝒜RT​(a⋆)=∑t=1TL¯t−infa∈𝒜∑t=1TLt​(a).R_{T}^{\mathrm{ext}}=\sup_{a^{\star}\in\mathcal{A}}R_{T}(a^{\star})=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\overline{L}_{t}-\inf_{a\in\mathcal{A}}\sum_{t=1}^{T}L_{t}(a). (33)

The infimum need not be attained.

Definition 4 excludes action-dependent state trajectories. For probability measures Q,PQ,P, define

KL(Q∥P)=∫log(d​Qd​P)dQ,\operatorname{KL}(Q\,\|\,P)=\int\log\!\left(\frac{\mathrm{d}Q}{\mathrm{d}P}\right)\,\mathrm{d}Q, (34)

when Q≪PQ\ll P, and +∞+\infty otherwise. Here Q≪PQ\ll P denotes absolute continuity and d​Q/d​P\mathrm{d}Q/\mathrm{d}P the relative density. For P=μP=\mu, KL measures prior-relative comparator complexity.

Exponential weights initialized by μ\mu uses the normalizer:

Zt=∫𝒜exp(−η∑r=1t−1Lr(a))dμ(a),Z_{t}=\int_{\mathcal{A}}\exp\!\left(-\eta\sum_{r=1}^{t-1}L_{r}(a)\right)\,\mathrm{d}\mu(a), (35)

and sampling measure ptp_{t} with density

d​ptd​μ​(a)=exp(−η∑r=1t−1Lr(a))Zt.\frac{\mathrm{d}p_{t}}{\mathrm{d}\mu}(a)=\frac{\exp(-\eta\sum_{r=1}^{t-1}L_{r}(a))}{Z_{t}}. (36)

Here Z1=1Z_{1}=1 and p1=μp_{1}=\mu. This update is measurable-space Hedge (Littlestone & Warmuth, 1994; Freund & Schapire, 1997; Cesa-Bianchi & Lugosi, 2006).

Theorem 1 gives the arbitrary-rate and optimized bounds. The proofs of the selection results below appear in Appendix B.2.

Corollary 2 (Product-prior complexity decomposition).

For 𝒜=𝒵×𝒲\mathcal{A}=\mathcal{Z}\times\mathcal{W}, μ=π⊗ρ\mu=\pi\otimes\rho, and finite-KL QQ with marginals QZ,QWQ_{Z},Q_{W},

KL(Q∥π⊗ρ)=KL(QZ∥π)+KL(QW∥ρ)+IQ(Z;W).\operatorname{KL}(Q\,\|\,\pi\otimes\rho)=\operatorname{KL}(Q_{Z}\,\|\,\pi)+\operatorname{KL}(Q_{W}\,\|\,\rho)+I_{Q}(Z;W). (37)

Here IQ=KL(Q∥QZ⊗QW)I_{Q}=\operatorname{KL}(Q\,\|\,Q_{Z}\otimes Q_{W}) measures comparator dependence, not loss interaction.

For a product comparator Q=QZ⊗QWQ=Q_{Z}\otimes Q_{W}, IQ​(Z,W)=0I_{Q}(Z;W)=0. A frozen language model can induce the text prior, while the parameter prior may encode rank, precision, sparsity, or provenance.

Corollary 3 (Prior-atom description-length regret).

Under the product prior μ=π⊗ρ\mu=\pi\otimes\rho, for positive-mass atoms z⋆,w⋆z^{\star},w^{\star}, put Cπ=−log⁡π⁡({z⋆})C_{\pi}=-\log\pi(\{z^{\star}\}) and Cρ=−log⁡ρ⁡({w⋆})C_{\rho}=-\log\rho(\{w^{\star}\}). Then RT​(z⋆,w⋆)≤(Cπ+Cρ)/η+η​T/8R_{T}(z^{\star},w^{\star})\leq(C_{\pi}+C_{\rho})/\eta+\eta T/8, optimized to T⁡(Cπ+Cρ)/2\sqrt{T(C_{\pi}+C_{\rho})/2} when the complexity is positive.

For an autoregressive language-model prior with almost-sure termination or bounded serialization length, CπC_{\pi} is a text description length. Zero-mass points have infinite pointwise KL, so they require a nearby positive-mass comparator and a regularity condition.

Corollary 4 (Local point regret on continuous spaces).

Let 𝒜=𝒵×𝒲\mathcal{A}=\mathcal{Z}\times\mathcal{W}, μ=π⊗ρ\mu=\pi\otimes\rho, and let dZ,dWd_{Z},d_{W} be metrics with measurable balls. Suppose every loss satisfies

|Lt​(z,w)−Lt​(z′,w′)|≤GZ​dZ​(z,z′)+GW​dW​(w,w′),|L_{t}(z,w)-L_{t}(z^{\prime},w^{\prime})|\leq G_{Z}d_{Z}(z,z^{\prime})+G_{W}d_{W}(w,w^{\prime}), (38)

for nonnegative GZ,GWG_{Z},G_{W} uniform over rounds. Fix a⋆=(z⋆,w⋆)a^{\star}=(z^{\star},w^{\star}) and radii δZ,δW>0\delta_{Z},\delta_{W}>0 whose balls 𝔹Z=B⁡(z⋆,δZ)\mathbb{B}_{Z}=B(z^{\star},\delta_{Z}) and 𝔹W=B⁡(w⋆,δW)\mathbb{B}_{W}=B(w^{\star},\delta_{W}) have positive respective prior mass. RT​(a⋆)≤CδZ,δW​(a⋆)η+η​T8+T⁡(GZ​δZ+GW​δW).R_{T}(a^{\star})\leq\frac{C_{\delta_{Z},\delta_{W}}(a^{\star})}{\eta}+\frac{\eta T}{8}+T(G_{Z}\delta_{Z}+G_{W}\delta_{W}). (39)

Shrinking the balls reduces localization loss but may increase complexity. For positive local complexity, optimizing η\eta gives

RT​(a⋆)≤T​CδZ,δW​(a⋆)2+T⁡(GZ​δZ+GW​δW).R_{T}(a^{\star})\leq\sqrt{\frac{TC_{\delta_{Z},\delta_{W}}(a^{\star})}{2}}+T(G_{Z}\delta_{Z}+G_{W}\delta_{W}). (40)

For mixed spaces, replace one ball by an atom. The bound is sublinear if CδZ,δW​(a⋆)=o⁡(T)C_{\delta_{Z},\delta_{W}}(a^{\star})=o(T) and GZ​δZ+GW​δW=o⁡(1)G_{Z}\delta_{Z}+G_{W}\delta_{W}=o(1). Without regularity, however, the distributional theorem does not control zero-mass points.

Learning-Rate and Computational Interpretation.

The arbitrary-η\eta result holds simultaneously over finite-KL comparators, whereas optimized rates are comparator-tuned. Grids, doubling, or parameter-free methods remove the need for advance knowledge at an additional regret cost (Orabona & Pál, 2016), although preserving low-refresh guarantees is nontrivial. The guarantee is statistical and does not require Gibbs normalization, sampling, or candidate proposal to be computationally efficient.

A.2.3 Mode Restriction and the Value of Joint Configurations

The all-admissible family values and gaps in Proposition 2 depend on Ξ\Xi, the evaluator, and TT, independently of hard-target feasibility; see Definition 3. Joint access need not measure interaction: L⁡(z,w)=1−0.4​z−0.4​wL(z,w)=1-0.4z-0.4w on {0,1}2\{0,1\}^{2} with base (0,0)(0,0) has a positive joint-effect gap but zero factorial interaction. These gaps also differ from finite-candidate restriction in the Spider comparison and per-use target discrepancy εe\varepsilon_{e}; see Appendix D for the latter.

For mode-restricted selection under the Cartesian specialization, use slice priors:

μZ\displaystyle\mu_{Z} =π⊗δw0on 𝒜Z,\displaystyle=\pi\otimes\delta_{w_{0}}\quad\text{on }\mathcal{A}_{Z}, (41)
μW\displaystyle\mu_{W} =δz0⊗ρon 𝒜W.\displaystyle=\delta_{z_{0}}\otimes\rho\quad\text{on }\mathcal{A}_{W}. (42)

These priors avoid conditioning on a possibly zero-mass product slice. Proposition 2 gives the exact selection–approximation–restriction identity and its EW bound. Appendix A.2.5 further splits comparator approximation into localization and discovery.

Corollary 5 (Mixture-prior mode selection).

Let ℰ⊆{Z,W,Z​W}\mathcal{E}\subseteq\{Z,W,ZW\} be nonempty, with priors μe\mu_{e} supported on 𝒜e\mathcal{A}_{e} and positive weights αe\alpha_{e} summing to one. Extend each mode prior by zero to the union and define

μmix=∑e∈ℰαe​μe.\mu_{\mathrm{mix}}=\sum_{e\in\mathcal{E}}\alpha_{e}\mu_{e}. (43)

EW with this mixture prior satisfies, for fixed finite-KL Qe≪μeQ_{e}\ll\mu_{e},

RT(Qe)≤(KL(Qe∥μe)+log(1/αe))/η+ηT/8.R_{T}(Q_{e})\leq(\operatorname{KL}(Q_{e}\,\|\,\mu_{e})+\log(1/\alpha_{e}))/\eta+\eta T/8. (44)

For e∈{Z,W}e\in\{Z,W\}, add the proposition’s approximation and restriction gaps to compare with the joint optimum.

Overlapping modes contribute additively to the mixture. Choosing μZ​W=π⊗ρ\mu_{ZW}=\pi\otimes\rho preserves (37).

To keep mode identity observable, use the tagged lift:

𝒜~ℰ\displaystyle\widetilde{\mathcal{A}}_{\mathcal{E}} =⨆e∈ℰ({e}×𝒜e),\displaystyle=\bigsqcup_{e\in\mathcal{E}}(\{e\}\times\mathcal{A}_{e}), (45)
μ~mix\displaystyle\widetilde{\mu}_{\mathrm{mix}} =∑e∈ℰαe​(δe⊗μe),\displaystyle=\sum_{e\in\mathcal{E}}\alpha_{e}(\delta_{e}\otimes\mu_{e}), (46)

with projected loss L~t​(e,a)=Lt​(a)\widetilde{L}_{t}(e,a)=L_{t}(a). EW samples (e,a)(e,a) and deploys aa, retaining mode identity where families overlap. The lifted comparator has exact KL

KL(δe⊗Qe∥μ~mix)=KL(Qe∥μe)+log(1/αe).\operatorname{KL}(\delta_{e}\otimes Q_{e}\,\|\,\widetilde{\mu}_{\mathrm{mix}})=\operatorname{KL}(Q_{e}\,\|\,\mu_{e})+\log(1/\alpha_{e}). (47)

Without tags, overlap can reduce KL, so this certificate need not identify a posterior mode cost.

Equal weights charge at most log⁡2\log 2 for two modes or log⁡3\log 3 with the joint mode, while approximation or restriction can remain Θ⁡(T)\Theta(T). Full-information integration neither proposes candidates nor certifies feasibility or deployment cost. Bandit variants additionally introduce action-set dependence (Auer et al., 2002; Bubeck & Cesa-Bianchi, 2012).

A.2.4 Joint and Coordinatewise Selection

Use the finite Cartesian family, product prior, exogenous loss table, full feedback, and common initialization of Section 3. For a positive deterministic learning-rate schedule ηt\eta_{t}, define the common target distribution:

qt​(z,w)=π(z)ρ(w)exp(−ηt∑r<tdr(z,w))∑(u,v)∈𝒞π(u)ρ(v)exp(−ηt∑r<tdr(u,v)).q_{t}(z,w)=\frac{\pi(z)\rho(w)\exp\!\left(-\eta_{t}\sum_{r<t}d_{r}(z,w)\right)}{\sum_{(u,v)\in\mathcal{C}}\pi(u)\rho(v)\exp\!\left(-\eta_{t}\sum_{r<t}d_{r}(u,v)\right)}. (48)

The constant choice ηt=η\eta_{t}=\eta recovers (3), whereas a varying ηt\eta_{t} rescales the entire cumulative loss. A sweep preserves qtq_{t} when initialized from it, but the preceding configuration need not have that law.

Additivity and a product prior factorize the EW target; see Proposition 3. Bounded multiplicative losses dt​(z,w)=gt​(z)​ht​(w)d_{t}(z,w)=g_{t}(z)h_{t}(w) generally do not factorize it, but nonadditivity alone need not separate regret.

Exact Constants for the Fixed-Rate Separation.

For the barrier loss ff of Proposition 4, the exact constants are as follows. For every fixed ηt=η>0\eta_{t}=\eta>0 and every T≥1T\geq 1, the selectors above satisfy

RTjoint\displaystyle R_{T}^{\mathrm{joint}} ≤3​Δ+2​b4+Δeη​Δ−1+2​(Δ+b)eη⁡(Δ+b)−1≤1+3η,\displaystyle\leq\frac{3\Delta+2b}{4}+\frac{\Delta}{e^{\eta\Delta}-1}+\frac{2(\Delta+b)}{e^{\eta(\Delta+b)}-1}\leq 1+\frac{3}{\eta}, (49)

Exact Constants for the Convergent Separation.

Under Corollary 1, the value of η1>0\eta_{1}>0 does not affect uniform initialization. For γ=Δ/b>1\gamma=\Delta/b>1 and T≥2T\geq 2,

RTjoint\displaystyle R_{T}^{\mathrm{joint}} ≤3​Δ+2​b4+Δ​4−γ​(1+1γ−1)+2​(Δ+b)​4−(γ+1)​(1+1γ),\displaystyle\leq\frac{3\Delta+2b}{4}+\Delta 4^{-\gamma}\left(1+\frac{1}{\gamma-1}\right)+2(\Delta+b)4^{-(\gamma+1)}\left(1+\frac{1}{\gamma}\right), (51)

These separations concern the specified conditional sampler, not arbitrary alternating optimization. More sweeps, global refreshes, or deliberate transitions through higher-loss configurations can change its behavior. Exact joint sampling may also be costly, and these results establish no computational advantage. The controlled selection study in Section 6 tests interaction, sweep count, and learning rate by exact probability propagation.

A.2.5 Candidate Proposal, Discovery, and Selection

Candidate construction uses scores, traces, gradients, or critiques (Zhou et al., 2023; Deng et al., 2022; Pryzant et al., 2023; Yang et al., 2024a; Guo et al., 2024; Fernando et al., 2024; Yüksekgönül et al., 2025; Lee et al., 2026a; Lee et al., 2026b). We separate discovery from selection on a fixed family. Changing families instead require tracking, sleeping-expert, or growing-expert guarantees (Herbster & Warmuth, 1998; Cortes et al., 2019; Mourtada & Maillard, 2017).

Let L^train\widehat{L}_{\mathrm{train}} and L^valid\widehat{L}_{\mathrm{valid}} denote empirical losses on the declared training and validation data. A bilevel joint proposal fits, for each proposed harness zz,

w^(z)≈arg⁡minw:(z,w)∈𝒜L^train(z,w),\widehat{w}(z)\approx\mathop{\arg\min}_{w:(z,w)\in\mathcal{A}}\widehat{L}_{\mathrm{train}}(z,w), (53)

then chooses

z^\displaystyle\widehat{z} ≈arg⁡minz:∃w⁡(z,w)∈𝒜L^valid(z,w^(z)),\displaystyle\approx\mathop{\arg\min}_{z:\,\exists w\ (z,w)\in\mathcal{A}}\widehat{L}_{\mathrm{valid}}\bigl(z,\widehat{w}(z)\bigr), (54)
a^\displaystyle\widehat{a} =(z^,w^​(z^)).\displaystyle=\bigl(\widehat{z},\widehat{w}(\widehat{z})\bigr). (55)

Outer validation search may be discrete and inner fitting gradient-based, but these approximate minimizations do not establish finite-budget convergence. Alternating procedures use (21)–(22): BetterTogether alternates prompt optimization and fine-tuning (Soylu et al., 2024), while WHALE alternates model updates and executable-harness search (Kim et al., 2026). They motivate, but differ from, the fixed-family conditional sampler in Section 3. Our guarantees apply after the family and prior are fixed.

For nonempty measurable 𝒞e=𝒞∩𝒜e\mathcal{C}_{e}=\mathcal{C}\cap\mathcal{A}_{e}, e∈{Z,W}e\in\{Z,W\}, define

VT,𝒞e\displaystyle V_{T,\mathcal{C}}^{e} =infa∈𝒞e∑t=1TLt​(a),\displaystyle=\inf_{a\in\mathcal{C}_{e}}\sum_{t=1}^{T}L_{t}(a), (56)
𝖣𝗂𝗌𝖼Te​(𝒞e)\displaystyle\mathsf{Disc}_{T}^{e}(\mathcal{C}_{e}) =VT,𝒞e−VTe≥0,\displaystyle=V_{T,\mathcal{C}}^{e}-V_{T}^{e}\geq 0, (57)

where QeQ_{e} is supported on 𝒞e\mathcal{C}_{e}. Discovery charges the candidate family’s gap to the all-admissible optimum VTeV_{T}^{e}, while localization charges QeQ_{e}’s gap to the best candidate in the family. Substituting 𝖠𝗉𝗑Te​(Qe)=ΛT,𝒞e​(Qe)+𝖣𝗂𝗌𝖼Te​(𝒞e)\mathsf{Apx}_{T}^{e}(Q_{e})=\Lambda_{T,\mathcal{C}}^{e}(Q_{e})+\mathsf{Disc}_{T}^{e}(\mathcal{C}_{e}) into (7) gives

∑t=1TL¯t−VTZ​W=\displaystyle\sum_{t=1}^{T}\overline{L}_{t}-V_{T}^{ZW}={} [∑t=1TL¯t−∑t=1T∫𝒞eLt​(a)​d​Qe​(a)]⏟selection+ΛT,𝒞e​(Qe)⏟localization\displaystyle\underbrace{\left[\sum_{t=1}^{T}\overline{L}_{t}-\sum_{t=1}^{T}\int_{\mathcal{C}_{e}}L_{t}(a)\,\mathrm{d}Q_{e}(a)\right]}_{\text{selection}}+\underbrace{\Lambda_{T,\mathcal{C}}^{e}(Q_{e})}_{\text{localization}}
+𝖣𝗂𝗌𝖼Te​(𝒞e)⏟discovery+Δemode​(T)+Δjoint​(T)⏟mode and joint restriction.\displaystyle+\underbrace{\mathsf{Disc}_{T}^{e}(\mathcal{C}_{e})}_{\text{discovery}}+\underbrace{\Delta_{e}^{\mathrm{mode}}(T)+\Delta^{\mathrm{joint}}(T)}_{\text{mode and joint restriction}}. (59)

A family prior controls only selection. Localization vanishes for a point mass on the best atomic candidate, while discovery remains relative to the proposals and budget. Non-Cartesian families require a joint prior and KL.

A.3 State Effects and Policy Regret

Bounded influence and full diagonal feedback control the state term in (2), and resets permit whole-episode policy selection. Section 5 weakens the feedback assumptions.

A.3.1 Persistent State and Policy Regret

Section 4 defines policy regret using each fixed comparator’s own trajectory. Propositions 5 and 6 show why evaluating all configurations on the learner’s state can conceal irreversible damage and why unrestricted persistent state precludes sublinear guarantees. The constructions and proofs are in Appendix B.3. Relabeling gives the parameter-only obstruction when that mode admits the same transitions, although actual text and parameter updates need not be symmetric.

A.3.2 Policy Regret under Bounded Influence

Bound each coordinate’s influence while allowing interactions within its history window (Arora et al., 2012; Anava et al., 2015). Fix a prior μ\mu on 𝒜=𝒵×𝒲\mathcal{A}=\mathcal{Z}\times\mathcal{W} or a measurable compatibility subset supporting every refresh.

The functions in Assumption 1 have domains

ft:𝒵min⁡{mZ+1,t}×𝒲min⁡{mW+1,t}→[0,1].f_{t}:\mathcal{Z}^{\min\{m_{Z}+1,t\}}\times\mathcal{W}^{\min\{m_{W}+1,t\}}\rightarrow[0,1]. (60)

Windows include the current coordinate, so zero horizon excludes carryover. Bundles use their largest horizon. For e∈{Z,W}e\in\{Z,W\}, write mem_{e} for its coordinate horizon, truncated at T−1T-1 without changing the windows.

For a=(z,w)∈𝒜a=(z,w)\in\mathcal{A}, define the diagonal loss:

dt​(a)=ft​(z,…,z⏟min⁡{mZ+1,t},w,…,w⏟min⁡{mW+1,t}).d_{t}(a)=f_{t}\!\left(\underbrace{z,\ldots,z}_{\min\{m_{Z}+1,t\}};\underbrace{w,\ldots,w}_{\min\{m_{W}+1,t\}}\right). (61)

This specializes (1). Assumption 2 requires valid simulation or cloning of each constant history. Ordinary full information on the learner’s realized history does not reveal these losses.

Lazy Exponential Weights.

Apply exponential weights (36) to the diagonal oracle, coupling draws by measurable Shrinking Dartboard to control state (Geulen et al., 2010; Kalai & Vempala, 2005). For η>0\eta>0, set Lt=dtL_{t}=d_{t} in (36) to define the target marginal qtq_{t}, and draw A1=(z1,w1)∼μA_{1}=(z_{1},w_{1})\sim\mu. qt+1​(d​a)\displaystyle q_{t+1}(\mathrm{d}a) =e−η​dt​(a)ζt​qt​(d​a).\displaystyle=\frac{e^{-\eta d_{t}(a)}}{\zeta_{t}}q_{t}(\mathrm{d}a). (63)

The lazy algorithm has marginals At∼qtA_{t}\sim q_{t}. For t=1,…,T−1t=1,\ldots,T-1,

𝔼⁡[Yt]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[Y_{t}] ≤min⁡{η​𝔼​[dt​(At)],1−e−η}≤η,\displaystyle\leq\min\left\{\eta\,\mathbb{E}[d_{t}(A_{t})],1-e^{-\eta}\right\}\leq\eta, (64)

To control the signed state effect isolated by Proposition 7, count departures from constant histories.

Under Assumption 1, for any realized sequence At=(zt,wt)A_{t}=(z_{t},w_{t}), put

χs=max{mZ𝟏{zs≠zs−1},mW𝟏{ws≠ws−1}},s=2,…,T.\chi_{s}=\max\left\{m_{Z}\mathbf{1}\{z_{s}\neq z_{s-1}\},m_{W}\mathbf{1}\{w_{s}\neq w_{s-1}\}\right\},\qquad s=2,\ldots,T. (66)

≤∑s=2Tχs.\displaystyle\leq\sum_{s=2}^{T}\chi_{s}. (67)

Theorem 2 combines these selection and contamination bounds, with the exact learning rate in (12).

For mixture prior (43), with each μe\mu_{e} supported on its slice 𝒜e\mathcal{A}_{e} and Qe≪μeQ_{e}\ll\mu_{e}, replace CQC_{Q} by

which is exact on the tagged lift and may exceed untagged KL. Whole-pair refreshes still charge mmaxm_{\max}, even when comparator complexity concentrates on one mode.

Under Theorem 2, suppose μ=π⊗ρ\mu=\pi\otimes\rho and the diagonal losses satisfy the Lipschitz condition of Corollary 4. For its metrics, positive-mass balls, and local complexity, every η>0\eta>0 gives

RTpol​(a⋆)≤CδZ,δW​(a⋆)/η+η⁡[T/8+mmax​(T−1)]+T⁡(GZ​δZ+GW​δW).R_{T}^{\mathrm{pol}}(a^{\star})\leq C_{\delta_{Z},\delta_{W}}(a^{\star})/\eta+\eta\left[T/8+m_{\max}(T-1)\right]+T(G_{Z}\delta_{Z}+G_{W}\delta_{W}). (70)

Proposition 8 in Section 4 gives the mode-restricted bounds for the supported slice priors (41)–(42). Zero KL permits a fixed prior draw, atoms give description lengths, and balls add localization. Proofs are in Appendix B.3.
